turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hi, sorry we're a few minutes late. The 405 was just stopped, and then we circled the parking garage twice.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're fine, we still have the slot. What brings him in?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Good morning, doctor. My skin itches.

[SEG0004] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah. He's six. Dry patches behind both knees and in the creases of his elbows, they itch, and it's worse at night. He scratches in his sleep, sometimes till it looks raw.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has this been going on?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): I am in first grade, doctor. I did my spelling words.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's nice to hear. I was asking about the rash, how many weeks. Mom, can you pin it down?
[SEG0008] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm. Five or six weeks, I think. I can't pin the exact day. It was after school started.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, five or six weeks of dry itchy patches behind the knees and elbows, worse at night, with scratching. Any fever?
[SEG0010] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. No fever.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): And eating, is his appetite off?
[SEG0012] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Appetite is fine. He eats.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough or wheezing, or anything else with his breathing or his chest?
[SEG0014] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No cough, no wheeze. Breathing is totally fine.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anywhere else on the skin, the face, the hands, the belly?
[SEG0016] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. Just those spots.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): What creams have you used?

[SEG0018] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Err, a white tube, hydrocortizone, the 1 percent. Once a day, when I remember, not every day honestly. Of. the blue tub, it's thick, I never learned the name. And a little yellow tube from my sister, we tried that twice and I stopped it.
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): I do not like the yellow one, doctor. It stings.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. So the hydrocortizone one percent is hit or miss, the blue tub has no name, and the yellow one is stopped because it stings. Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0021] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. None.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Family history, asthma, eczema, allergies in the parents?
[SEG0023] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His father has asthma. He uses an inhaler. I don't.

[SEG0024] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh, and his dad was gonna drive, but the car is in the shop on account of the brakes. The game was on the radio the whole way, Dodgers were up by three, and we talked about that inning for ten minutes in the elevator. That wind in the lot was something too. Silly, I know.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sounds like a full morning. Let's come back to him. Has he been to school?
[SEG0026] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He missed a couple days last week. Otherwise he goes.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, I've had a look. Dry thickened patches in both elbow creases and behind both knees, some scratch marks. No weeping. I don't see any infection.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. It tickles.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): This looks like eczema to me, atopic dermatitis. Dad's asthma fits that picture. It's a working impression, not something I'm calling final today.
[SEG0030] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Okay.

[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thursday morning the nurse takes bloods, an eosinophil count and a serum IgE, to back up this eczema impression. Be here at 8. He does not need to fast, breakfast as usual. No cream on the arms that morning until after they've drawn it.
[SEG0032] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thursday, eight, breakfast yes, no cream till after.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): If those bloods are borderline, then we do a skin-prick panel. I'm not booking that today.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): And if the rash does not settle, we'll do a skin scraping for fungus. Only in that case.
[SEG0035] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Right.

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm changing the steroid. Stop the hydrocortizone one percent. I'll start triamcinalone, and I almost said zero point one percent, but for him it should be zero point zero two five percent cream, thin layer, twice a day, for two weeks, only on the rough patches.
[SEG0037] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Twice a day, thin, two weeks. What about the blue tub?

[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't use the blue tub. Use plain petrolatum, like Vaseline, at least 3 times a day and right after every bath, lukewarm water about ten minutes, pat dry, ointment on within three minutes. Cotton pajamas, nails short, and mittens at night are fine if he scratches. I'll see you in two weeks, and if it starts weeping or he gets a fever, call us before that.

spec.situation: Mother brings a child with itchy dry patches behind the knees and elbows, worse at night, scratching; creams named by colour; father has asthma; doctor adjusts steroid cream and moisturiser advice.

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

traps.happens: The transcript looks like speech-to-text: drug names are sometimes spelled wrongly ('Omprazole', 'Mizartan' for telmisartan, 'Metformine'), fragments and fillers appear ('Err', 'Of.', 'Mm.', 'Umm'), numbers are sometimes digits and sometimes words.
traps.label_rule: Medicine names are recorded as written in the transcript (name) with a normalized/generic name ONLY when the true drug is certain from context (a drug 'for the pressure' written 'Mizartan' is NOT certain enough: leave generic_name empty). Fragments and fillers are never facts.

features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.

bad.reason: Patient reports yellow cream stings, but not that stinging is resolved.
Transcript only states no medicine allergies, not all allergies.
Blue tub is stopped by doctor, not reported discontinued by family member.
Doctor notes some scratch marks, but body site for scratch marks isn't separately specified.

omissions.text: The itching leads to scratching in sleep, sometimes until the skin looks raw.
No other breathing/chest problems were reported in addition to no cough and no wheeze ('Breathing is totally fine').
Hydrocortisone 1% had been used inconsistently: once a day only when remembered, not every day.
The yellow tube cream had only been tried twice before being stopped because it stung.
The doctor specifically noted the skin-prick panel is not being booked today.
